'''''Maranta leuconeura''''', widely known as the '''prayer plant''' due to its daily sunlight-dependent movements (which are said to resemble hands "in-prayer"), is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Marantaceae]] [[native plant|native]] to the [[Brazil]]ian [[tropical forest]]s.<ref name="marynatalizia"/> It is a variable, [[rhizomatous]] [[perennial plant|perennial]], growing to {{convert|30|cm|0|abbr=on}} tall and broad, with crowded clumps of evergreen, strikingly-marked oval leaves, each up to {{convert|12|cm|0|abbr=on}} long. The plant spreads itself horizontally, carpeting an entire small area of [[forest floor]], sending roots into the substrate at each [[Node (plant)|leaf node]].

''Maranta'', in-addition to fellow "prayer-plant" genera (like ''[[Calathea]]'',  ''[[Ctenanthe]]'',  ''[[Goeppertia]]'' and ''[[Stromanthe]]''), is related to such groups as ''[[Alpinia]]'',  ''[[Ensete]]'', ''[[Canna (plant)|Canna]]'',  ''[[Curcuma]]'', ''[[Heliconia]]'',  ''[[Musa (genus)|Musa]]'' and  ''[[Zingiber]]''.

==Description==
The [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''leuconeura'' means "white-veined", referring to the leaves.<ref name=RHSLG>{{cite book|last=Harrison|first=Lorraine|title=RHS Latin for gardeners|year=2012|publisher=Mitchell Beazley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=9781845337315|pages=224}}</ref> The leaves have a habit of lying flat during the day, and folding in an erect position at night as if in prayer for evening vespers,<ref name="Encyclopaedia Britannica">{{cite web|author=((Britannica Editors))|title=Prayer plant|url=https://www.britannica.com/plant/prayer-plant|website=Plant|publisher=Encyclopaedia Britannica|accessdate=3 December 2017}}</ref> hence the common name "prayer plant".<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book|title=RHS A-Z encyclopedia of garden plants|year=2008|publisher=Dorling Kindersley|location=United Kingdom|isbn=978-1405332965|pages=1136}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Missouri Botanical Garden - ''Maranta leuconeura''|url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/gardens-gardening/your-garden/plant-finder/plant-details/kc/b604/maranta-leuconeura.aspx|accessdate=24 May 2013}}</ref> This behaviour is an example of a [[diurnal rhythm]].

Small, white to purple flowers appear during the growing season, although this is not always observed in houseplants and the flowers may not be considered significant in comparison to the attractive foliage.<ref name="Missouri Botanical Garden">{{cite web|last1=Missouri Botanical Garden|title=Maranta leconeura|url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=b604|website=Gardening help|accessdate=3 December 2017}}</ref> The broad leaves of the plant are oval, two-color, greenish and fairly shiny. There are patches on both sides of the leaf medium, the color of which varies depending on the variety. The patches may be light green, green, brownish or dark gray. Medium color also varies by variety. The undersides of the leaves are variable, ranging from a light green, common in ''M. leuconeura'' var. ''kerchoveana'', to a deep red, common in ''M. leuconeura'' var. ''erythroneura''. Roots are shallow.<ref name="Brickell" />

Flowers, although small, are interesting in that they have a trigger mechanism, closing the entrance to the flower quickly with a curling appendage, which both deposits and collects pollen in one motion, and only triggers once per flower, as for others in this plant family.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Ley |first1=Alexandra C. |last2=Claßen-Bockhof |first2=Regine |title=Pollination syndromes in African Marantaceae |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/24428532 |website=ResearchGate}}</ref> Flowers open in the morning, one or two at a time per cassette, and wilt in the evening, falling off if not pollinated. Each capsule may contain ten or so flowers, so a capsule may last over a week with daily flowers. Each flower stalk has two capsules, one below the other.

==Cultivation==
[[File:Maranta-timelapse.gif|thumb|left|''Maranta leuconeura'' var. ''erythroneura'' (prayer plant) "praying", i.e., raising its leaves for the evening|alt=]]
''Maranta leuconeura'' is a well-known [[houseplant]] in [[temperateness|temperate]] regions, requiring a minimum temperature of {{convert|15|C|F|abbr=on}}. As a plant that is native to rainforests, ''Maranta'' prefers bright indirect sunlight, high humidity, and well-drained soil that has a high humus content.<ref name="Missouri Botanical Garden"/> Acidic, clay or loam soils are tolerable.<ref name=Edward>{{cite web|last1=Gilman|first1=Edward|title=Maranta leuconeura|url=http://hort.ifas.ufl.edu/shrubs/MARLEUA.PDF|website=University of Florida Cooperative Extension Service|accessdate=3 December 2017}}</ref>

Direct sunlight should be avoided, as well as standing water. At daytime the ideal temperature is 21–27 °C and at night 16–21 °C; the night temperature should not be lower than 15 °C. Higher temperatures also require higher humidity, for example, just spraying. Due to the thin leaves of this species and their need for high humidity, prolonged dry and arid conditions as well as excessive sunlight can damage the plants. [[File:Damaged Lemon-Lime Maranta Leuconeura or Prayer Plant 01.jpg|thumb|Lemon-Lime cultivar of the Maranta Leuconeura species, featuring necrosis at the margins.]]

During the growing season, spring and summer, ''Maranta'' houseplants require moist soil and fertilization every month. Slightly drier soils and reduced fertilizer application are recommended for the remainder of the year.<ref name="Missouri Botanical Garden"/> In warmer climates, at USDA Zones 10b-11,<ref name=Edward /> it can be grown as [[groundcover]] in moist, shady areas.

===Propagation===
Spacing between plants should be between {{convert|60|and|90|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}}<ref name=Edward /> Propagation is achieved via division and [[cuttings (plant)|cuttings]].<ref name="Missouri Botanical Garden"/> Cuttings, 10 cm in length with 3–4 leaves, should be taken in the spring. Bottom heat can be applied to the cuttings to promote rooting.<ref name="Brickell" /> Propagation by seed is possible although is less common. Seed germination is recommended at {{convert|13|–|18|C|F}}.<ref name="Brickell">{{cite book|last1=Brickell|first1=Christopher|last2=Zuk|first2=Judith|title=The American Horticultural Society A-Z Encyclopedia of Garden Plants|date=1997|publisher=DK Publishing|location=New York, Ny|isbn=0-7894-1943-2|edition=1st|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/americanhorticul00chri}}</ref> ''Maranta leuconeura'' can also be propagated [[in vitro]].<ref name="Ebrahim">{{cite journal|last1=Ebrahim|first1=Mohsen|last2=Ibrahim|first2=Ibrahim|title=InØuence of medium solidiÆcation and pH value on in vitro propagation of Maranta leuconeura cv. Kerchoviana|journal=Scientia Horticulturae|date=12 February 2000|volume=2000|issue=86|pages=211–221|url=https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/6c0b/95286c3ce2af267720a11a40efd86623106f.pdf|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171204061406/https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/6c0b/95286c3ce2af267720a11a40efd86623106f.pdf|url-status=dead|archive-date=4 December 2017|accessdate=3 December 2017|doi=10.1016/s0304-4238(00)00148-5|s2cid=30459427}}</ref>

==Common uses==
''M. leuconeura'' can be grown in planters, hanging baskets, mass planting, and as an edging plant.<ref name=Edward /> This plant is frequently used in shopping malls.<ref name=Edward />

==Chemistry==
[[Rosmarinic acid]] can be found in plants in the family Marantaceae such as ''Maranta leuconeura''.<ref>Occurrence of rosmarinic acid, chlorogenic acid and rutin in Marantaceae species. Yana Abdullah, Bernd Schneider and Maike Petersen, Phytochemistry Letters, 12 December 2008, Volume 1, Issue 4, Pages 199–203, {{doi|10.1016/j.phytol.2008.09.010}}</ref>

==Diseases==
''Maranta'' usually experiences minimal insect pest pressure, however, [[spider mites]] and [[mealybug]]s can be of significant concern.<ref name="Missouri Botanical Garden"/> [[Leaf spot]] and [[cucumber mosaic virus]] are diseases that can occur.<ref name="Brickell" /> [[Root rot]] can occur in poorly drained soils.<ref name="Missouri Botanical Garden"/>
